1.1.1.title: Non-text Content
1.1.1.why: Screen reader users hear nothing, or a file name, for images, icons and icon-only buttons that have no text alternative, so they cannot tell what the thing is or does.

1.2.1.title: Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded)
1.2.1.why: People who are deaf cannot hear audio-only content and people who are blind cannot see video-only content unless a transcript or audio track is provided.

1.2.2.title: Captions (Prerecorded)
1.2.2.why: People who are deaf or hard of hearing miss everything said in a video that has no captions.

1.2.3.title: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded)
1.2.3.why: People who are blind miss information that a video only shows visually.

1.2.4.title: Captions (Live)
1.2.4.why: People who are deaf cannot follow live audio without real-time captions.

1.2.5.title: Audio Description (Prerecorded)
1.2.5.why: People who are blind miss on-screen actions and text in video unless it is described in the audio.

1.2.6.title: Sign Language (Prerecorded)
1.2.6.why: For many Deaf people sign language is their first language and captions are harder to follow.

1.2.7.title: Extended Audio Description (Prerecorded)
1.2.7.why: When pauses are too short to describe the visuals, blind users still miss information unless the video pauses for description.

1.2.8.title: Media Alternative (Prerecorded)
1.2.8.why: People who are deafblind need a full text alternative to read with a braille display.

1.2.9.title: Audio-only (Live)
1.2.9.why: People who are deaf cannot follow a live audio stream without a text alternative.

1.3.1.title: Info and Relationships
1.3.1.why: When headings, lists, tables, labels and groups are only visual, screen reader users lose the structure that sighted users rely on, such as which label belongs to which field.

1.3.2.title: Meaningful Sequence
1.3.2.why: Screen readers read in DOM order; if that differs from the visual order in a way that changes meaning, the content becomes confusing or wrong.

1.3.3.title: Sensory Characteristics
1.3.3.why: Instructions like 'tap the gold button on the right' are useless to people who cannot see colour, shape or position.

1.3.4.title: Orientation
1.3.4.why: People with devices mounted to a wheelchair, or who cannot rotate their phone, are locked out if the app only works in one orientation.

1.3.5.title: Identify Input Purpose
1.3.5.why: Without autocomplete tokens, browsers and assistive tools cannot autofill personal details, which is a real barrier for people with memory, motor or cognitive disabilities.

1.3.6.title: Identify Purpose
1.3.6.why: Landmarks and programmatic purposes let people use tools that simplify or re-skin pages and jump between regions; without them every page must be read top to bottom.

1.4.1.title: Use of Color
1.4.1.why: People who are colour blind cannot tell which item is selected, required or in error when colour is the only signal.

1.4.2.title: Audio Control
1.4.2.why: Audio that plays on its own drowns out the screen reader, so the user cannot hear how to stop it.

1.4.3.title: Contrast (Minimum)
1.4.3.why: Low-contrast text is hard or impossible to read for people with low vision, colour blindness or anyone outdoors on a phone. Normal text needs 4.5:1, large text 3:1.

1.4.4.title: Resize Text
1.4.4.why: People with low vision zoom to 200%; if text is clipped, overlaps or cannot grow, they cannot read it.

1.4.5.title: Images of Text
1.4.5.why: Text baked into an image cannot be resized, recoloured or read in a custom font by people who need to adjust text.

1.4.6.title: Contrast (Enhanced)
1.4.6.why: People with moderately low vision need stronger contrast than the AA minimum: 7:1 for normal text and 4.5:1 for large text.

1.4.7.title: Low or No Background Audio
1.4.7.why: Background music or noise makes speech hard to understand for people who are hard of hearing.

1.4.8.title: Visual Presentation
1.4.8.why: People with dyslexia or low vision need to choose colours, keep lines short, avoid justified text and have generous line and paragraph spacing to read comfortably.

1.4.9.title: Images of Text (No Exception)
1.4.9.why: Any text inside an image, except logos, cannot be adapted by people who need larger or differently styled text.

1.4.10.title: Reflow
1.4.10.why: At 320 CSS pixels wide (400% zoom on a laptop) content must fit without sideways scrolling; otherwise low-vision users scroll back and forth on every line.

1.4.11.title: Non-text Contrast
1.4.11.why: Input borders, icons, focus rings and control states below 3:1 are invisible to many people with low vision, so they cannot find or operate the control.

1.4.12.title: Text Spacing
1.4.12.why: People with dyslexia often increase letter, word, line and paragraph spacing; if content is clipped or overlaps when they do, they lose text.

1.4.13.title: Content on Hover or Focus
1.4.13.why: Tooltips and popovers that vanish when the pointer moves onto them, cannot be dismissed, or cover content make life hard for magnifier and keyboard users.

2.1.1.title: Keyboard
2.1.1.why: People who cannot use a mouse or touchscreen (keyboard, switch, voice control users) are completely blocked from any feature that only works with a pointer.

2.1.2.title: No Keyboard Trap
2.1.2.why: If keyboard focus can get into a component but not out, a keyboard user is stuck and must reload the page.

2.1.3.title: Keyboard (No Exception)
2.1.3.why: Every function, with no exceptions for path-dependent input, must work from a keyboard so nobody is left out.

2.1.4.title: Character Key Shortcuts
2.1.4.why: Single-letter shortcuts fire by accident for speech-input users, whose dictated words become key presses.

2.2.1.title: Timing Adjustable
2.2.1.why: People who read slowly, use screen readers or have motor disabilities need more time; messages or sessions that disappear on a timer take information away before they can use it.

2.2.2.title: Pause, Stop, Hide
2.2.2.why: Moving, blinking or auto-updating content distracts people with attention disorders and can make the rest of the page unusable for screen reader users.

2.2.3.title: No Timing
2.2.3.why: Any time limit at all can exclude someone; at AAA, timing must not be essential to the task.

2.2.4.title: Interruptions
2.2.4.why: Unrequested updates and pop-ups break concentration and can reset a screen reader user's place on the page.

2.2.5.title: Re-authenticating
2.2.5.why: If a session expires and the user loses what they typed, slower users are punished repeatedly.

2.2.6.title: Timeouts
2.2.6.why: People who need breaks deserve to be warned how long inactivity is allowed before data is lost.

2.3.1.title: Three Flashes or Below Threshold
2.3.1.why: Content that flashes more than three times a second can trigger seizures.

2.3.2.title: Three Flashes
2.3.2.why: At AAA no content may flash more than three times per second, regardless of size or colour.

2.3.3.title: Animation from Interactions
2.3.3.why: Motion triggered by scrolling or clicking can cause nausea, dizziness and migraines for people with vestibular disorders; they need a way to turn it off, usually via prefers-reduced-motion.

2.4.1.title: Bypass Blocks
2.4.1.why: Without a skip link or landmarks, keyboard and screen reader users must tab through the whole header on every page to reach the content.

2.4.2.title: Page Titled
2.4.2.why: The page title is the first thing a screen reader announces and how people find the right tab; a missing or stale title leaves them unsure where they are.

2.4.3.title: Focus Order
2.4.3.why: When Tab moves focus in an illogical order, or focus is lost after a dialog or route change, keyboard users get disoriented and may miss content.

2.4.4.title: Link Purpose (In Context)
2.4.4.why: Screen reader users often list links out of context; a link with no name, or one named only by an icon, gives them no idea where it goes.

2.4.5.title: Multiple Ways
2.4.5.why: Some people navigate by search, others by a site map or menu; offering more than one way helps people with different cognitive and visual needs.

2.4.6.title: Headings and Labels
2.4.6.why: Vague or missing headings and labels make it hard for everyone, and especially screen reader and cognitive-disability users, to know what a section or field is.

2.4.7.title: Focus Visible
2.4.7.why: Keyboard users need to see where focus is; without a visible indicator they are typing blind.

2.4.8.title: Location
2.4.8.why: People with cognitive disabilities benefit from always knowing where they are in the site, through breadcrumbs, a current-page marker or a descriptive title.

2.4.9.title: Link Purpose (Link Only)
2.4.9.why: At AAA a link's text alone, without the surrounding sentence, must say where it goes, so 'Learn more' and 'Click here' are not enough.

2.4.10.title: Section Headings
2.4.10.why: Headings let people skim and jump between sections; long unsectioned content is hard to navigate.

2.4.11.title: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
2.4.11.why: If a sticky header, footer or banner completely covers the focused element, keyboard users cannot see what they are on.

2.4.12.title: Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced)
2.4.12.why: At AAA no part of the focused element may be hidden by author-created content.

2.4.13.title: Focus Appearance
2.4.13.why: A thin or low-contrast focus ring is still hard to see for low-vision keyboard users; the indicator must be at least as large as a 2px outline around the control and change contrast by at least 3:1.

2.5.1.title: Pointer Gestures
2.5.1.why: Pinch, swipe or multi-finger gestures exclude people with tremors or who use a head pointer; a single-tap alternative is needed.

2.5.2.title: Pointer Cancellation
2.5.2.why: Actions that fire on press instead of release cannot be undone by sliding off, so people with tremors trigger things by accident.

2.5.3.title: Label in Name
2.5.3.why: Voice control users say what they see; if the accessible name does not contain the visible label, the command 'click Continue' does nothing.

2.5.4.title: Motion Actuation
2.5.4.why: Shake or tilt features cannot be used by people whose device is mounted, and can be triggered by tremors; they need a UI alternative and a way to disable motion.

2.5.5.title: Target Size (Enhanced)
2.5.5.why: Targets smaller than 44 by 44 CSS pixels are hard to hit for people with tremors, limited dexterity or large fingers.

2.5.6.title: Concurrent Input Mechanisms
2.5.6.why: People switch between touch, mouse, keyboard and voice; content must not lock them into one input method.

2.5.7.title: Dragging Movements
2.5.7.why: Dragging is hard or impossible for people with motor impairments; anything done by dragging must also be possible with single taps or clicks.

2.5.8.title: Target Size (Minimum)
2.5.8.why: Targets smaller than 24 by 24 CSS pixels, without enough space around them, cause mis-taps for people with limited dexterity.

3.1.1.title: Language of Page
3.1.1.why: Screen readers choose a voice and pronunciation from the page language; the wrong lang makes Spanish read with English rules, which is unintelligible.

3.1.2.title: Language of Parts
3.1.2.why: Passages in a different language from the page need their own lang so screen readers pronounce them correctly.

3.1.3.title: Unusual Words
3.1.3.why: Jargon and idioms block people with cognitive disabilities and second-language readers unless definitions are available.

3.1.4.title: Abbreviations
3.1.4.why: Unexplained abbreviations such as EBT or CVC confuse people who do not already know them.

3.1.5.title: Reading Level
3.1.5.why: Text above a lower-secondary reading level needs a simpler version for people with reading or cognitive disabilities.

3.1.6.title: Pronunciation
3.1.6.why: Where pronunciation changes meaning, screen reader users and people with reading disabilities need it provided.

3.2.1.title: On Focus
3.2.1.why: If moving focus onto something submits a form, opens a window or jumps the page, keyboard users get unexpected changes they did not ask for.

3.2.2.title: On Input
3.2.2.why: Changing a setting should not navigate or submit without warning; screen reader users may not notice the context changed.

3.2.3.title: Consistent Navigation
3.2.3.why: Navigation that moves around between pages forces people with low vision or cognitive disabilities to relearn each page.

3.2.4.title: Consistent Identification
3.2.4.why: When the same function has different names or icons on different pages, users cannot build a reliable mental model.

3.2.5.title: Change on Request
3.2.5.why: New windows or automatic redirects that the user did not ask for disorient screen reader and cognitive-disability users; links that open new tabs must say so.

3.2.6.title: Consistent Help
3.2.6.why: People who need help must find contact or help options in the same place on every page.

3.3.1.title: Error Identification
3.3.1.why: If an error is shown only by colour or not tied to the field, people cannot tell what went wrong or where.

3.3.2.title: Labels or Instructions
3.3.2.why: Placeholder text disappears on typing and is not a label; without labels and format hints, people do not know what to enter.

3.3.3.title: Error Suggestion
3.3.3.why: A message like 'invalid' without saying how to fix it leaves people with cognitive disabilities stuck.

3.3.4.title: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)
3.3.4.why: Payments and other important submissions must be reversible, checked or confirmed, because a mis-tap can cost someone money.

3.3.5.title: Help
3.3.5.why: Context-sensitive help on forms reduces errors for people with cognitive and learning disabilities.

3.3.6.title: Error Prevention (All)
3.3.6.why: At AAA every submission must be reversible, checked or confirmable so mistakes can be caught.

3.3.7.title: Redundant Entry
3.3.7.why: Asking for the same information twice in one process is a burden for people with memory and motor disabilities; it should be auto-filled or selectable.

3.3.8.title: Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
3.3.8.why: Logins that require remembering or transcribing codes without allowing paste or autofill block people with cognitive disabilities.

3.3.9.title: Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)
3.3.9.why: At AAA no cognitive function test, including recognising objects or personal content, may be required to log in.

4.1.2.title: Name, Role, Value
4.1.2.why: Assistive technology can only operate a control it can identify; custom controls without a role, name or state are invisible or misleading to screen reader and voice users.

4.1.3.title: Status Messages
4.1.3.why: Success messages, errors, loading and counts that appear without moving focus must be announced, or screen reader users never learn they happened.

1.4.3.note: Large text is at least 24px, or at least 18.66px and bold (font-weight 700 or more).

2.5.8.note: Undersized targets pass if a 24px circle centred on the target does not intersect another target or its circle (spacing exception), or another exception applies.

2.4.13.note: Indicator area at least that of a 2 CSS px perimeter of the unfocused component, with at least 3:1 contrast between focused and unfocused states.
